title: Start with a practical assessment of the site
focus: Review the kitchen, storage, service area and expected daily covers before choosing a management model. A menu cycle, staffing plan and commercial arrangement need to work together within those facilities. Define who supplies and maintains equipment, how meals are paid for and how changes in volume are handled. If a payment system is required, discuss it alongside the food operation. The written specification should make the responsibilities and review process clear before the service begins.

sections.title: Understand the workforce before setting the service
paragraphs: Daily meal demand depends on attendance, working patterns and the alternatives available to employees. Share typical occupancy, shift times and likely peak periods rather than the building capacity alone. If people have short or staggered breaks, the layout and menu should help them collect a meal within that window.

Discuss the balance between familiar daily choices and menu rotation. A staff survey or existing uptake figures can help inform the brief, while a trial provides a practical way to assess portion expectations and popular dishes. Menu decisions should still be reviewed against the agreed dietary requirements and available kitchen facilities.

Decide how feedback reaches the operator and who can approve changes. A regular review with facilities or the workplace team helps connect employee experience to staffing, service hours and the menu cycle. Clear responsibilities make the arrangement easier to improve without introducing conflicting instructions from several contacts.

sections.title: Allocate every facility responsibility
paragraphs: A canteen assessment should cover preparation space, refrigeration, cooking and holding equipment, dishwashing, storage and the movement of staff and diners. Existing equipment needs to be reviewed for the proposed operation. An empty room may require specialist design input and relevant approvals before a setup scope can be confirmed.

Record who provides and maintains each part of the facility. Utilities, cleaning, pest management, waste arrangements and equipment repairs may sit with different parties, but the operating plan needs a clear owner for each. Confirm how faults are reported and how any interruption to normal service will be handled.

The dining area also shapes the experience. Review queues, payment or collection points, seating and tray return. A practical route through the space helps keep the service comfortable at peak times and gives staff room to replenish and clear without crossing the busiest customer flow.

sections.title: Choose a commercial model with clear assumptions
paragraphs: A subsidised meal arrangement, fixed operating fee and revenue model distribute costs and responsibilities differently. Discuss how employees pay, what the organisation contributes and whether there is a minimum volume assumption. The written proposal should explain the chosen structure in terms finance and facilities can both use.

Separate ongoing operating costs from setup or equipment work. Confirm staffing hours, menu scope, consumables and any technology charges, together with how VAT is presented. If demand changes, the agreement should explain when pricing or service capacity will be reviewed rather than leaving either party to assume the original plan still applies.

Agree a launch and review programme before a longer commitment. Measure meal uptake, service times, feedback and operational requirements during the introduction period. Document any adjustments and their effect on the scope or price. A managed canteen works best when the daily experience and commercial assumptions are reviewed together.
